summary: Defines an SMTP extension that lets a sender ask for delivery status notifications under chosen conditions. The sender can say whether the original message should be returned and can attach identifying information to help match a report to a message. It was replaced by RFC 3461.

eli5.summary: When you mail a package, you can ask the post office to send back a note saying it arrived or got lost. This lets email senders ask for that kind of note.

questions: how to request delivery receipts in smtp
what is a delivery status notification
how does email forwarding handle dsn
subtitle: Let email senders request delivery status notifications under chosen conditions.

tldr.problem: Email senders and receivers need reliable notification of delivery success or failure, with a standardized format that can survive forwarding and gatewaying to foreign mail systems.
tldr.mechanism: Adds optional parameters to SMTP's MAIL and RCPT commands: NOTIFY (which conditions trigger a status report), ORCPT (original recipient address for tracking), RET (whether to return full message or just headers), and ENVID (envelope identifier to track the transaction).
tldr.outcome: Provides standardized delivery status notifications that are reliable, stable, and preserve enough information to match a DSN to its original message even after forwarding. Replaced by RFC 3461.

today: RFC 1891 is an Internet Standard but is obsoleted by RFC 3461, which is the current specification for SMTP delivery status notifications. The core mechanism remains the same; RFC 3461 clarifies and extends the original.

sections.title: Delivery Notifications in SMTP
sections.content:
The SMTP protocol requires that an SMTP server notify the sender if it cannot deliver a message to a recipient. Traditionally, that notification is an ordinary email message sent to the sender's address, containing an explanation and at least the headers of the failed message.

But experience with large mailing lists showed this is not enough: it is hard to know which recipient failed, at which host a problem occurred, or even whether a message arrived at an intermediate gateway. Without a standardized format, different mail systems generate different notifications that are difficult to parse or exchange with foreign systems. This memo defines an SMTP extension to solve these problems.
sections.eli5: Regular bounce messages are messy and hard to understand. This defines a standard way for mail servers to tell senders: "Your message got here," "It failed," or "Delivery is delayed."

sections.title: The Four DSN Parameters
sections.content:
The extension adds four optional parameters to SMTP commands. On the MAIL command, a sender specifies:

  • RET: Request either the full message (FULL) or just headers (HDRS) to be returned with a failure notification.
  • ENVID: A sender-chosen identifier (up to 100 characters) to track this transmission. The value is returned unchanged in any DSN, allowing the sender to match the notification to the original send.

On the RCPT command, for each recipient:

  • NOTIFY: Specify when DSNs should be issued. Values are NEVER (no notification), SUCCESS (notify on successful delivery), FAILURE (on delivery failure), DELAY (if delivery is delayed), or combinations like SUCCESS,FAILURE.
  • ORCPT: The original recipient address. When a message is forwarded or gatewayed to another system, the RCPT TO value may change, but ORCPT preserves what the sender originally specified, encoded as 'xtext' to handle non-ASCII characters.
sections.eli5: The sender tells the mail server: what kind of receipt to send back (NOTIFY), whether to send the full email or just the headers (RET), who really sent it (ENVID), and who the original addressee was (ORCPT).

sections.title: How DSNs Are Generated and Relayed
sections.content:
When a server receives a message with DSN parameters, it processes them as follows:

Successful delivery to a local recipient: If the recipient requested SUCCESS in NOTIFY, the server issues a delivered DSN saying the message arrived in the recipient's mailbox.

Delivery failure: If delivery fails and the recipient requested FAILURE, a failed DSN is issued describing the reason (bad address, unreachable host, etc.). If NOTIFY was absent, a failed DSN must still be issued as the default.

Relaying to other servers: When an SMTP server relays the message to another server that supports DSN, it propagates the same ENVID, RET, NOTIFY, and ORCPT parameters unchanged. If relaying to a server that does not support DSN, the relaying server must generate synthetic DSNs on behalf of the downstream server.

Forwarding and aliases: When a message is forwarded from an alias to a new recipient, the ENVID, RET, and ORCPT parameters are typically not propagated. The server may issue a relayed DSN to indicate the message left its control and went to another system.
sections.eli5: When mail arrives, the server checks what notifications were requested and sends them back. If mail goes to another server, the original sender's requests go along. If the next server doesn't understand DSN, the first server makes up the status report itself.

sections.title: The Format and Content of a DSN Message
sections.content:
A DSN is sent as a MIME message of type multipart/report with report-type delivery-status. It has three parts:

  • A human-readable explanation (plain text).
  • A message/delivery-status body containing machine-readable fields: Reporting-MTA (the server that generated the DSN), Original-Envelope-ID (the ENVID if one was supplied), Original-Recipient (the ORCPT), Final-Recipient (actual delivery address), Action (one of: delivered, failed, delayed, relayed, expanded), and Status (a three-part code like 2.0.0 for success or 5.0.0 for permanent failure).
  • The original message or its headers, depending on RET and whether delivery succeeded.

The DSN is sent with a null reverse-path (<>) so that if the DSN itself cannot be delivered, no loop of notifications occurs.
sections.eli5: A DSN is an email with three attachments: a note for humans, structured data for programs, and a copy of what happened to the original email.

sections.title: Implementation Rules and Limits
sections.content:
An SMTP server conforming to this spec must accept certain minimum parameter sizes: ENVID up to 100 characters, NOTIFY up to 28 characters, ORCPT up to 500 characters, and RET up to 8 characters. The entire SMTP command line must be at least 1036 characters long to accommodate combinations of these parameters.

When forwarding a message to an alias with multiple recipients, the server has three choices: omit the DSN parameters for all but one forwarding address, or propagate them to all addresses and issue a relayed or expanded DSN for the alias address itself. For mailing lists, the envelope return address is rewritten to the list maintainer, and the DSN parameters are reset; the list server issues a delivered DSN to the original sender, then the list members receive the message with new DSN requests determined by the list.

A conforming MTA never loops: if a DSN itself cannot be delivered, no secondary DSN is issued. Instead, the local postmaster is informed via a mechanism that will not itself generate DSNs.
sections.eli5: Servers have to handle long commands with lots of parameters. They follow strict rules so mail loops don't happen: if a status report bounces, they tell a human, not the computer.
